lesson.topicTitle: 1. Structure, Bonding & Introduction to Organic Chemistry

specAnchors.text: understand how ionisation energies are influenced by the number of protons in the nucleus, the electron shielding and the sub-shell from which the electron is removed
understand reasons for the trend in ionisation energy down Groups 1 and 2

primer.text: First ionisation energy measures the pull a gaseous atom exerts on its outermost electron. Across period 2 or 3 the general trend climbs as nuclear charge rises, radius shrinks and shielding stays put, with two small dips where a new subshell opens or pairing begins. Down any group the trend falls because added shells lengthen the nucleus-to-electron distance and thicken shielding. This note maps both directions and the four famous dips.

modules.title: The climb across a period
modules.opening: Moving left to right along period 2 or period 3, first ionisation energy climbs a broad staircase. Protons join the nucleus while the new electrons slot into the same outer shell, so attraction strengthens, atoms contract and the outer electron becomes progressively harder to detach. This lesson fixes the three factors behind that climb.
keyPoints: Across a period the nuclear charge rises because protons are added to the nucleus.
The atomic radius falls as the strengthened pull drags the outer shell inward.
Shielding by inner-shell electrons stays roughly level while electrons enter the same shell.
Removing the outer electron therefore costs more energy at every step across a period.
Group 1 metals sit low on the plot while noble gases reach the highest values.

low.restatement: As you cross a period, atoms keep adding protons and outer electrons to the same shell, so the pull grows, the atom shrinks and the first electron costs more to remove.
low.analogy: Picture a magnet under a sheet of paper with iron filings on it: more magnet strength with the paper thickness unchanged lifts every filing harder, just as extra protons grip the same shell more tightly.
low.examPointer: Quote all three factors when explaining the climb - nuclear charge up, radius down, shielding constant - markers look for the trio.

medium.restatement: The cross-period increase in first ionisation energy is a competition the nucleus wins: proton count grows while the added electron joins an already occupied shell, leaving distance and shielding near constant.
medium.analogy: Think of a loan shark raising the interest rate while the repayment schedule stays fixed: the same outer electron faces a stronger demand every step across the period.
medium.examPointer: When a question hands you a plot of values across a period, anchor your explanation on rising nuclear charge with essentially constant shielding - that pairing earns the marks.

modules.title: The two famous dips
sourceHeadings: Dips in the trend for period 2
Dips in the trend for period 3
modules.opening: Two kinds of wrinkle interrupt the cross-period climb in both periods 2 and 3: a small drop when the first electron enters a new p subshell, and a second when pairing forces two electrons to share an orbital. Beryllium-to-boron and nitrogen-to-oxygen in period 2 replay as magnesium-to-aluminium and phosphorus-to-sulfur in period 3.
keyPoints: A dip follows beryllium and magnesium because their next electron opens the p subshell, sitting further out than the filled s subshell.
A dip follows nitrogen and phosphorus because each next electron must pair in a p orbital, and spin-pair repulsion eases removal.
Period 2 dips: beryllium 900 to boron 800, nitrogen 1400 to oxygen 1310, in kJ mol^-1.
Period 3 dips: magnesium 738 to aluminium 578, phosphorus 1012 to sulfur 1000, in kJ mol^-1.
The dip mechanism is subshell geometry, not any change in shielding or nuclear charge.

low.restatement: Two spots in each period break the climb: starting a p subshell costs less than expected, and doubling up in a p orbital invites repulsion that helps the electron leave.
low.analogy: Moving into a new office floor takes less effort than squeezing a second colleague into an already occupied desk - the paired-up worker is the first to quit.
low.examPointer: Name the mechanism for each dip type separately: subshell distance for Be-B and Mg-Al, spin-pair repulsion for N-O and P-S.

medium.restatement: The dips are electronic-structure fingerprints: a 2p or 3p electron is higher in energy than a filled s subshell, and a paired p electron adds mutual repulsion, so either way the measured ionisation energy lands below the neighbour before it.
medium.analogy: A commuter penalty: changing trains (new subshell) or sharing a cramped seat (paired orbital) both make the journey easier to abandon than the smooth run before it.
medium.examPointer: Configurations win marks: quote 1s2 2s2 for beryllium against 1s2 2s2 2px1 for boron when explaining that dip.

modules.title: The slide down a group
sourceHeadings: Summary Explanation for Trend in Ionisation Energy Across a Period and Down a Group
modules.opening: Descend any group and first ionisation energy falls at every step. The nucleus gains protons, yet each new element wraps its outer electron in an extra shell: the electron stands further away behind thicker shielding, and those two effects swamp the extra charge. This lesson assembles the full four-factor argument.
keyPoints: First ionisation energy decreases down a group.
Nuclear charge rises down a group as protons are added.
Atomic radius grows because each element down the group adds a shell of electrons.
The nucleus-to-outer-electron distance and the shielding both increase down the group.
The distance and shielding gains outweigh the extra nuclear charge, easing removal.

low.restatement: Going down a column, the outer electron sits on a further-out shell behind more screening, so it leaves more easily even though the nucleus is more charged.
low.analogy: A whisper from the front of a hall barely reaches the back rows: extra rows (shells) and more people in front (shielding) drown out the louder voice (extra protons).
low.examPointer: Always concede the rising nuclear charge before overruling it with distance and shielding - answers that skip the concession lose marks.

medium.restatement: Down-group decline is a weighted sum: proton count adds attraction, but an extra shell adds distance and screening, and the product of those two dominates the electrostatic balance that binds the outer electron.
medium.analogy: Two friends pulling a rope towards you versus the rope getting longer and a colleague leaning on the middle: length plus slack beats the extra puller.
medium.examPointer: For 'explain the trend down group 2' style questions, order the argument: charge up, radius and distance up, shielding up, therefore removal easier.

glossary.definition: The energy needed to remove one outer electron from each gaseous atom of an element, quoted in kJ mol^-1.
The screening of the outer electron from nuclear attraction by inner-shell electrons.
The extra repulsion between the two electrons sharing one orbital, which eases removal of a paired electron.
The repeating pattern of chemical and physical properties shown by elements across the periods of the periodic table.
